50b3f9051389: Tradition Two answers one question for every A.A. group: who decides? The Long Form (Big Book, p. 563): "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience." Ultimate authority means the last word, and in a group's business no person holds it. The threat it answers is a boss. Bill W. wrote in 1947 (A.A. pamphlet P-17, p. 37): "Time out of mind, families, friends, employers, doctors, clergymen, and judges have tried their hand at disciplining alcoholics. Almost without exception the failure to accomplish anything by coercion has been complete." Coercion means forcing. Every drunk who walks in has already been bossed by experts, and it didn't work. Put a boss over the group and he meets one more person trying to run him, and he leaves. So Bill drew the line: "the only real authority to be found in A.A. is that of spiritual principle. It is never personal authority." That tells no one what to believe. It takes power away from whoever wants it. Today the boss often comes built in: a counsellor at the front of the room, a program that sets the rules, a court that wants a signature. Test it tonight: ask who has the last word in your room, and whether the answer is a person.

928fedecf060: A group can keep the letter of Tradition Two, take a vote, and still break itself, by forcing a split decision through on one count. By spring the six have stopped coming, and two of them have started a meeting across town. Nobody broke a rule. But the group's conscience is the members together, and half of them just walked out. The member close behind, never thrown away. The danger was never one person with an opinion. It was a room splitting into camps until nobody was left to answer the phone. Today the charge is often lit from outside: a program wants the meeting, and the members split over whether to let it have it. Test it tonight: if your group blew apart tomorrow, which piece would the next drunk still find with its doors open?

2f0fa2a092c2: A shared disaster can fill a room, but the Big Book says it was never what held A.A. together. The Big Book (p. 17): "We are like the passengers of a great liner the moment after rescue from shipwreck when camaraderie, joyousness and democracy pervade the vessel from steerage to Captain's table." Steerage was the cheapest deck. Then the warning: "The feeling of having shared in a common peril is one element in the powerful cement which binds us. The Long Form asks for a whole that lives on its own (Big Book, p. 563): "A.A. must continue to live or most of us will surely die." A requirement can't keep a group alive. Test it tonight: if every court slip and facility van stopped tomorrow, would your group still have enough members to open its doors?

The group has outgrown its room, and newcomers stand along the back wall. A bigger hall is free on the same night. The group's best-known member, twenty years sober, says he won't follow.
